title: From Request Fulfillers to Outcome Owners
leaves: Agreement on the why. A named steering group and advisory group. A date for the first direction review.

slides.html:
From Request Fulfillers
To Outcome Owners

Digital services at the DMV
slides.notes: Open conversationally. This is a conversation starter, not a reorganization announcement. The aim is to name what we all already feel, explain why it happens, and show a proven way to work differently, one success at a time.

slides.html:
Does this feel familiar?

Endless request queue

We're buried in feature requests with no clear way to know which ones will actually make a difference for the community.

Timeline extension

A project's timeline and budget are re-estimated halfway through, forcing our partners to scramble and eroding their trust in our ability to deliver.

"Successful" failures

We deliver a project on time and on budget, but our partners are still unhappy and the core problem isn't truly solved.

IT "black box"

Our partners see us as an order-taking group that's slow to respond, and our staff feels like they're just closing tickets instead of thinking strategically.
slides.notes: Name the pain before naming any fix. Let the room nod. These are symptoms of the model, not of the people: we have a big team full of committed individuals.

slides.html: How we think we work
slides.notes: The assembly line: requirements go in one end, a finished product comes out the other. Each station does its part and hands off. It looks orderly and predictable.

slides.html: How we actually work
slides.notes: The telephone game. Each handoff changes the message a little, and by the end of the line nobody is building what the first person meant.

slides.html:
How we
should work
slides.notes: The soccer team. The goal is fixed and everyone can see it. The path to it changes every few seconds, and each player adapts. That is outcomes over outputs.

slides.html:
We are pulled in every direction

Success is defined by our ability to appease competing stakeholders, not by the impact we deliver.

Our teams spend their energy balancing internal priorities, not maximizing public value.

There's no single, clear direction of "forward."
slides.notes: Today several people each hold a "number one" priority, and the team picks by the biggest fire. Nobody is doing anything wrong; the system has no single direction of forward.

slides.html:
Two competing systems

Projects

One system provides "project" work and has its own specific process with roles and responsibilities.

Operations

Another system is managed by different people with different processes, roles and responsibilities.

The challenge

People are caught in between these two systems, and have no way to reconcile them.
slides.notes: Software used to come in a box. Today it is continuous, with no finish line. We still fund it, build it and "operationalize" it, so people get caught between a project system and an operations system.

slides.html:
Temporary efforts vs enduring value

Project

A temporary effort to deliver a specific output, like a system upgrade, a new feature, or an installation. It has a defined start and end.

Product (or service)

An ongoing thing you build that delivers value to people. It's ongoing and evolves.

Projects aren't the problem; they fit work with a clear end. Our problem: we also treat enduring services (like HR systems, data and analytics, or a resident-facing service) like temporary projects. We fund them, build them, and "operationalize" them, but the user's need for them is continuous, evolving and always increasing.
slides.notes: Swap in the services this audience knows best. Say the fit point out loud: a system upgrade or a hardware refresh is a project and should run as one. The trouble is running a service that never ends as if it will.

slides.html:
The shift that changes everything

From project to product, for the work that never ends

ProjectProduct
MindsetOutputsOutcomes
GoalDeliver a thingCreate a change
MetricOn time, on budget, built to specMeasurable improvement in a user or business metric
"We built what you asked for.""We achieved the outcome you need."
slides.notes: The DMV story works here: "We launched online renewal on schedule, all requirements met" is the output. "Six months later, 75% of renewals are done online in under five minutes" is the outcome. Use a story from your own service if you have one. Both columns are real ways of working. Expect "so projects are bad now?" and answer no: this is about which one fits the work.

slides.html:
Our process reflects our mindset

Traditional process

Waterfall

"Big upfront requirements, big risk, and we only find out if we were right at the very end."

Iterative delivery

Wagile (fake agile)

"This is agile in name only. We're just building a predefined plan faster. It's a faster assembly line, but we're still building the wrong car if the plan was wrong."

Product focus

Lean, HCD, Agile

"This is where we need to go. A continuous flow where we discover, deliver, and learn. This allows us to adapt and ensures we're always working on the most valuable thing."
slides.notes: Point back to the assembly line on slide 3: wagile makes it faster without asking whether we're building the right car. Waterfall isn't wrong for fixed, well-understood work like an installation; it's the wrong fit for a service that keeps changing.

slides.html:
This is happening

This isn't a radical experiment; it's about adopting a proven model for public service.

The City of Philadelphia, for example, is building internal teams focused on improving services before applying new technology, a core tenet of the product mindset.

Franklin County, Ohio has reorganized to focus on digital services, with product managers leading application development teams.

Colorado and Pennsylvania have both established state-level digital services to keep offering better digital experiences to their residents.

This is the model used in the private sector as well as at the federal level (USDS, 18F), and across the United Kingdom and Canada.
slides.notes: Check these examples still hold before presenting: federal digital service teams changed in 2025, and a leader may ask. Add a local example if you have one.

slides.html:
Right now, we're organized around projects and departments. This creates silos and handoffs.

A better model is organizing around value streams: the end-to-end activities that deliver value to a customer (a community member or internal user).

This means shifting from temporary project teams to persistent, long-lived teams that own an outcome.

Portfolio / BSA

PMO

Development

Value stream A

Value stream B

Value stream C
slides.notes: Today work moves down the columns: portfolio, PMO, development, each with its own handoff. A value stream cuts across them, one team carrying an outcome end to end. Check the column names match how your IT organization is set up today.

slides.html:
Everything fits in a value stream

CommunityStaffEnabling
FocusDelivering services directly to the public.Empowering DMV employees to do their jobs effectively.Providing foundational platforms for all other streams.
ExampleA resident's journey to renew a vehicle registration without a trip to the office.The internal HR system used for payroll.The secure network, cloud infrastructure, and developer tools.
GoalImprove public access and community outcomes.Improve internal efficiency and effectiveness.Increase the speed, reliability, and security of all teams.
slides.notes: The community example is the DMV's. Pick the resident journey this audience will recognize fastest.

slides.html:
Not just for websites

Enterprise systems (HR, payroll)

This is a staff value stream. The "product" is the employee's experience. The "outcome" is less time on admin and better workforce planning.

Data and BI

This is an enabling value stream. The "product" is the organization's ability to make decisions. The "outcome" is a measurable improvement in a department's key measure.

Vehicle renewals

This is a community value stream. The "product" is a resident's journey to renew without a trip. The "outcome" is fewer trips to the office and fewer calls asking how.
slides.notes: Swap the examples for the systems and services this audience knows best; a real one in the room beats a good one from elsewhere.

slides.html:
A shift in our roles

This new model doesn't change who our people are; it changes the system they work in. It lets us redirect their valuable expertise to a more impactful set of roles.

FromTo
Documenting requirements given to us by stakeholders.Investigating the underlying problems to make sure we're solving the right thing.
Managing fixed schedules and delivering a predefined scope.Facilitating the continuous flow of value and adapting to what we learn.
Tracking the status of disconnected projects.Guiding strategic investments to achieve measurable outcomes for the people we serve.
slides.notes: This is the reassurance slide. Nobody's job disappears; the work gets more interesting. Expect "where do I fit?" and answer it directly.

slides.html:
How we make this transition

This transformation isn't a top-down reorganization. It's a movement that proves its value one success story at a time.

1 / Pilot

We start with one or two teams. We give them the air cover to work in this new way. We let them demonstrate what's possible.

2 / Attract

Pilot success creates demand. We use the wins to change the conversation from "what do you want?" to "what outcome can we achieve together?"

3 / Scale

We scale only after we've proven it works here, in our own culture, and have a repeatable pattern for success.
slides.notes: The pilot is the one team that works this way first. Name what starts first: a rehearsal quarter of planning, capacity shares, and a weekly request review. Once other departments see results, they will want to work this way too.

slides.html:
Better value, less risk, happier people

This new model directly solves our most common frustrations.

Reducing risk

Continuous feedback stops us building the wrong thing. We can deliver value sooner.

Increasing value

An outcome focus means we're always working on the most important problem.

Improving partnerships

We become true partners with the business, sharing ownership of the results.

Empowering staff

We elevate our teams from specialists to strategic problem solvers, increasing job satisfaction.
slides.notes: Tie each benefit back to a pain from slide 2: risk to timeline extensions, value to the endless queue, partnerships to the black box, staff to closing tickets.

slides.html:
Challenges

People change

This deeply affects people and how they see themselves within the system, and people generally don't like change.

We have to treat this change on the most human level possible: be open, listen, and communicate.

Financial framework

The way budgeting and accounting work is a structure that fights against this model.

We have to spend time with finance so the way our finances are set up ties costs to the value delivered.

Optics

This is a very new way of showing value. Results come sooner, but the reporting can feel counterintuitive at first.

We have to be transparent, communicate, and revamp how we report on our progress and our value.
slides.notes: Say these out loud before anyone else does. With this audience the financial framework one lands hardest: projects are how budgets work today. Optics: early reporting can look worse before it looks better.

slides.html: Questions?
slides.notes: Close with: this is a conversation starter. Ask what would make them confident enough to give one team air cover for a quarter.

pain.description: Name the pain leaders already feel: the request queue, slipping timelines, successful failures, IT as a black box.

cause.description: Why it happens: pulled in every direction, two competing systems, and treating enduring services like temporary projects.

shift.description: The shift from project to product, and proof that public organizations already work this way.

path.description: What changes for our people, how we make the transition, what we gain and what will be hard.
